teaser: A life-size nude with tangled hair and no goddess to excuse her. Paris argued about her for months.
review_notes:
Dimensions given as about 129.5 x 195.6 cm (Met).
Claim that Courbet's 1864 Salon submission (Venus and Psyche) was rejected for indecency.
Claim that Courbet said Count Nieuwerkerke had promised to buy the painting for the state and then backed out.
Cezanne carrying a photograph of the picture in his wallet is a reported anecdote (repeated by the Met).
Manet's Young Lady in 1866 was shown at the Salon of 1868 and is also at the Met; reading it as a reply to Courbet is a common interpretation, not a documented fact.
The object at lower right is described only as a trailing ribbon or strip of cloth; it is hard to identify in the image.

lesson.text: This canvas is almost two meters wide, about 1.3 by 1.95 meters (roughly 4 by 6.5 feet). That means the woman lying across it is the size of a real person. Stand in front of it at the Met and she is not a figure in a picture. She is someone in the room with you.

In 1866, a nude this large was perfectly acceptable in Paris, on one condition. She had to be somebody else: Venus, a nymph, a bather from ancient Rome. The official yearly exhibition, called the Salon, was full of smooth, hairless goddesses floating on waves. Myth was the alibi that made bare skin respectable.

Gustave Courbet gives you no alibi. He had spent fifteen years insisting that painting should show only what the painter can see, an idea people called Realism. So where a goddess should be, he paints a woman on a rumpled bed. Three areas of the canvas made that hard to ignore.

lesson.title: No goddess here
lesson.text: Three places where Courbet refuses to tidy things up.

spots.title: The hair
spots.text: Brown curls spill in every direction over the white sheet, almost to the bottom edge. Salon goddesses had hair arranged like sculpture. Critics singled out this mess as improper.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Her head tips back toward you, upside down, lips parted in a smile. She is watching the bird, not posing for the viewer. Her mood is private and playful.

spots.title: The sheet
spots.text: The linen is creased and dragged half off the bed, painted in thick grays and whites. This is an unmade bed in a real room, not a cloud or a seashell.

lesson.text: Tangled hair, a laughing mouth, a bed that has been slept in: critics of 1866 complained about exactly these things. They called the pose ungainly and the hair disheveled. What bothered them was not nudity. It was that this body looked as if it belonged to the present day.

Two years earlier, the Salon jury had turned down a Courbet nude for indecency. Woman with a Parrot was his way back in: it was the first of his nudes the jury accepted, and it hung in front of the crowds of 1866.

To get past the jury, Courbet borrowed the tools of the very painters he mocked. The skin is smooth and pale, the background is dark and rich, and the whole body is arranged with great care. The pose looks like an accident. It is anything but.
Follow the structure hiding under that careless sprawl.

lines.label: The body
lines.text: From the feet on the right, the body rises to the hip and then slopes down to the head. Her head is the lowest point: she tips toward you, which is why she seems to slide out of the picture.

lines.label: The arm
lines.text: One arm shoots straight up from the shoulder. It is the only vertical in the lower half, and it carries your eye from her face to the bird.

lines.label: The wings
lines.text: The parrot's open wings make a small bright bar at the top, the only strong color against the dark. It lands on her fingers like the last note of a phrase.

lesson.text: So the eye travels in a loop: along the legs, down to the face, up the arm, out to the wings. Around that loop Courbet keeps everything dim. A heavy patterned hanging closes off the room, and only a slice of daylit trees shows in the top left corner.
Courbet kept the polish of an academic nude but removed the myth. What shocked people was not a naked body. It was a naked body with no story to hide behind.

Courbet claimed that the count who ran the fine arts administration had promised to buy the painting for the French state, then backed out. The painter was furious and complained loudly in public letters. He kept the canvas and showed it again in his own private pavilion in 1867.

And the parrot? Pet parrots were fashionable in Paris apartments, a luxury brought from far away. In older paintings a bird can stand for a lover or a confidant. Courbet does not say. He does, however, show you where the bird lives.
The parrot has just flown from its perch. Where is the perch?

spots.title: The empty perch
spots.text: A tall wooden stand with pegs like a ladder, topped by a small feeding dish. It is nearly lost in the dark. The bird has crossed the entire width of the canvas to reach her hand.

lesson.text: That flight from the stand to her hand is the only event in the painting. One younger painter took the hint. Edouard Manet soon painted his own woman with a parrot: fully dressed in a pink gown, standing, cool and upright. Many see it as his dry reply to Courbet. Today the two canvases hang in the same museum.
Paul Cezanne is reported to have carried a small photograph of this painting in his wallet.

The picture crossed the Atlantic with the Havemeyers, New York collectors who built a fortune in sugar and bought Courbet when few Americans dared. It came to the Metropolitan Museum in 1929 with the bequest of Louisine Havemeyer.

Which brings you back to the size. A small nude can be a jewel, something to own. A life-size one stares the room down. Courbet wanted the argument to happen at full scale, and he signed it in red in the bottom left corner, with the date: 66.

quiz.question: Why was a nude usually acceptable at the Paris Salon?
options: If it was painted very small
If it showed a goddess or a figure from myth
quiz.explanation: Myth served as the excuse that made bare skin respectable.

quiz.question: What did critics of 1866 complain about in this painting?
options: The ungainly pose and disheveled hair
The bright colors of the parrot
quiz.explanation: They attacked the awkward pose and the messy hair, which made her look like a woman of the present day.

quiz.question: Where is the parrot's perch?
options: Behind her head on the left
On the far right, a tall stand with pegs
quiz.explanation: The stand with its feeding dish is on the right, nearly lost in the dark.

quiz.question: Which painter answered with his own woman with a parrot, this time fully dressed?
quiz.explanation: Manet painted a standing woman in a pink gown with a parrot.

quiz.question: What is the lowest point of the woman's body in the composition?
quiz.explanation: Her head tips back toward the viewer, below the level of her hips and feet.

facts.text: The woman in the painting is roughly life-size.
facts.explanation: The canvas is almost two meters wide, so the figure is the size of a real person.

facts.text: The Salon jury rejected Woman with a Parrot in 1866.
facts.explanation: It was accepted, the first of Courbet's nudes to pass the jury.

facts.text: Courbet presents the woman as the goddess Venus.
facts.explanation: He gives her no mythological identity, which is what unsettled viewers.
